binders: A real-valued random variable X with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
Independent sample variables X_1,...,X_N, each drawn from the distribution of X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
An accuracy tolerance epsilon > 0, as required for the interval (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon) to express an accuracy radius (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).

A failure parameter delta for which log(delta^{-1}) and the target probability 1-delta are meaningful; the intended range is 0 < delta < 1, though it is not printed explicitly (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
hypotheses: The observations are independent and identically distributed with the law of X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The variance sigma^2 = Var X is finite so that the stated finite order bound in sigma^2/epsilon^2 applies (Exercise 2.2.9(a)-(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).

Each weak estimate used in the median construction is the part-(a) estimate, obtainable from a block of O(sigma^2/epsilon^2) observations and epsilon-accurate with probability at least 3/4 (Exercise 2.2.9(a), footnote 2, and the hint to part (b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
conclusions: There is an estimator computed from the sample, specifically obtainable by taking the median of O(log(delta^{-1})) weak estimates from part (a), whose total sample size is N = O(log(delta^{-1}) sigma^2/epsilon^2) (Exercise 2.2.9(b) and its hint, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
That estimator is epsilon-accurate with probability at least 1-delta (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).

By the exercise's definition, epsilon-accurate means that the estimator lies in the open interval (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon), equivalently has absolute error strictly less than epsilon (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
definitions_and_conventions: mu denotes the mean of X and sigma^2 denotes Var X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a), PDF page 7; printed page 18).

A weak estimate is the part-(a) sample-mean estimate with success probability at least 3/4 and sample order sigma^2/epsilon^2 (Exercise 2.2.9(a), its hint and footnote 2, PDF page 7; printed page 18).

The median construction uses independent weak estimates formed from the independent sample, naturally by disjoint blocks; the disjoint-block realization is an analyst-explicit implementation of the hint, not additional printed wording (hint to Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The O-notation hides absolute numerical constants; this is explicitly stated for part (a) in footnote 2 and is naturally inherited by part (b)'s two O-expressions (PDF page 7; printed page 18).
implicit_context: Exercise 2.2.9(b) inherits the estimation problem, iid sampling model, definition of epsilon-accuracy, and notation mu and sigma^2 from the opening paragraph and part (a) on the same page.

The requested median amplification relies on concentration of the number of failed weak estimates; it is placed immediately after Hoeffding's inequality and its applications, although part (b) states only the construction hint rather than a named bound.
The source's phrase 'from part 1' in the part-(b) hint refers structurally to part (a), the only preceding part of this exercise.

details: The conclusion concerns existence/computability of an estimator from the observed sample, not concentration of the raw sample mean at confidence 1-delta (Exercise 2.2.9(b) and hint, PDF page 7; printed page 18).

The median is taken over weak estimates based on independent sample data, so the boosting probability is with respect to the joint sample law (Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part-(b) hint, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The main exercise defines accuracy by the strict interval (mu-epsilon, mu+epsilon), hence |estimate-mu| < epsilon (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
Footnote 2 uses the weak inequality |mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon when spelling out part (a), creating a boundary-convention discrepancy relevant to exact formalization (PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The total number of observations scales as the product log(delta^{-1}) sigma^2/epsilon^2 up to an absolute multiplicative constant (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The hinted decomposition is O(log(delta^{-1})) blocks, each supporting a weak estimate at O(sigma^2/epsilon^2) sample cost (parts (a)-(b) and hints, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The boosted estimator's success probability is at least 1-delta, including equality at the stated lower bound (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The weak estimates need only the part-(a) success guarantee of at least 3/4 before median amplification (Exercise 2.2.9(a) and part-(b) hint, PDF page 7; printed page 18).

undebatable_constraints: The data X_1,...,X_N are independent draws from the distribution of X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening, PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The target mean is mu = E X and the variance parameter is sigma^2 = Var X (Exercise 2.2.9 opening and part (a), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The estimator must be computable from a total sample of order log(delta^{-1}) sigma^2/epsilon^2 (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
Its probability of being epsilon-accurate must be at least 1-delta (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
The hinted estimator is the median of order log(delta^{-1}) weak estimators from part (a), rather than merely the unboosted full-sample mean (hint to Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
Every weak estimate has the part-(a) scale O(sigma^2/epsilon^2) and success probability at least 3/4 (Exercise 2.2.9(a), its footnote, and the part-(b) hint, PDF page 7; printed page 18).

ambiguities.issue: The source does not explicitly state the admissible range of delta.
ambiguities.evidence: Part (b) writes log(delta^{-1}) and success probability at least 1-delta but supplies no printed quantifier or interval for delta (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
ambiguities.impact: The natural range is 0 < delta < 1, but for delta near 1 the raw logarithm can be too small to encode even one block unless a ceiling, additive constant, or max{1,log(1/delta)} convention is supplied; an exact theorem must state a range and rounding convention.

ambiguities.issue: The O-notation and integer sample/block counts do not specify constants or rounding.

ambiguities.impact: A formal statement must choose absolute constants and natural-number ceilings (and ordinarily an odd positive number of blocks for an unambiguous median) while preserving the asserted order bound.

ambiguities.issue: The printed accuracy convention differs between the exercise opening and footnote 2.
ambiguities.evidence: The opening defines epsilon-accuracy using the open interval (mu-epsilon,mu+epsilon), whereas footnote 2 spells the part-(a) event as |mu-hat-mu| <= epsilon (PDF page 7; printed page 18).
ambiguities.impact: For distributions with atoms at the error boundary, strict and non-strict events need not coincide. The main part-(b) phrase 'epsilon-accurate' points to the opening strict definition, but a formalization should record its chosen boundary convention.

ambiguities.issue: Degenerate zero variance is not reconciled with an integer sample-size formula proportional to sigma^2.
ambiguities.evidence: The displayed order in part (b) is log(delta^{-1}) sigma^2/epsilon^2 without an additive baseline, and no exception for sigma^2=0 is stated (Exercise 2.2.9(b), PDF page 7; printed page 18).
ambiguities.impact: Taken literally at sigma^2=0, the bound suggests zero observations even though the unknown constant mean is learned from a draw; exact formulations generally require at least one observation or treat the order statement asymptotically/nondegenerately.

contract_plain_english: For a real random variable X of finite variance sigma squared and iid observations from its law, estimate its mean mu to within epsilon. Part (a) gives a weak sample-mean estimator using order sigma squared over epsilon squared observations and succeeding with probability at least 3/4. Part (b) asks to form order log(1/delta) independent weak estimates and take their median. With a total of order log(1/delta) times sigma squared over epsilon squared observations, this estimator must fall within the epsilon-neighborhood of mu with probability at least 1-delta. The source leaves the exact constants, integer rounding, delta range, and a strict-versus-nonstrict boundary convention implicit or inconsistent.
